quickstart/agent-driven-build:
This track treats the sandbox as an agent's tool environment. You can supply the intelligence from your own backend, or use the Agent Runs API when you want MIOSA to dispatch OSA, Claude Code, Codex, or another harness against a sandbox or computer target. For the managed runner path, see [Agent Runs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs) and [Agent Run Groups](/docs/api-reference/agent-run-groups). To try a harness from the terminal first, follow [Quickstart, step 3](/docs/quickstart#3-run-an-agent-inside-it). ## Pick a harness A harness is the coding agent that MIOSA runs inside the sandbox. You pick it with the `runner` field. The agent uses your own model account, never MIOSA credits. | Agent | `runner` | Connect your account | |---|---|---| | OSA | `osa` | Connect your model key in the console, under **Agents**. | | Claude Code | `claude-code` | `miosa connections add models claude` (your plan) or `anthropic` (your key). | | Codex | `codex` | `miosa connections add models chatgpt` (your plan) or `openai` (your key). | | OpenCode | `opencode` | `miosa connections add models chatgpt`, `openrouter` or `anthropic`, then `miosa connections use opencode --all`. | | Kimi Code | `kimi` | `miosa connections add models kimi` (your plan). | | Pi | `pi` | `miosa connections add models anthropic`, `chatgpt` or `openrouter`, then `miosa connections use pi --all`. | | Mistral | `mistral` | `miosa connections add models vibe` (your plan) or `mistral` (your key). | | Hermes | `hermes` | `miosa connections add models chatgpt` (your plan) or `anthropic` / `openai` / `openrouter` (your key). | Run one from your backend: **TypeScript** ```typescript const run = await sandbox.run("Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000", { runner: "osa", // or "claude-code", "codex", "opencode", "kimi", "pi", "mistral" }) console.log(run.status) ``` **Python** ```python run = sandbox.run_agent( "Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000", runner="osa", # or "claude-code", "codex", "opencode", "kimi", "pi", "mistral" ) print(run["status"]) ``` If the account for that harness is not connected, MIOSA refuses the run and says what to connect. You do not need the console to connect one. Set a key or connect a Claude or ChatGPT plan from your own code, for your workspace or for each of your end users: [Connect agent accounts](/docs/guides/connect-agent-accounts). **TypeScript** ```typescript await miosa.connections.setKey({ provider: "anthropic", key: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY! }) // A customer's own Claude plan, used only for runs on their machines const signin = await miosa.connections.connectSubscription({ provider: "claude", externalUserId: "user-456" }) console.log(signin.verificationUrl) // show it in your UI, then: await signin.submitCode(pastedCode) ``` **Python** ```python miosa.connections.set_key("anthropic", key=os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]) # A customer's own Claude plan, used only for runs on their machines signin = miosa.connections.connect_subscription("claude", external_user_id="user-456") print(signin.verification_url) # show it in your UI, then: signin.submit_code(pasted_code) ``` ### Step 1 - Create a sandbox with external attribution. If you're embedding MIOSA in your own product, pass your user/project IDs so you can filter resources later. **TypeScript** ```typescript const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox", workspaceSlug: "default", // the MIOSA workspace it belongs to wait: true, // hold the call until the sandbox is ready externalWorkspaceId: "acct-123", // your own grouping id, not a MIOSA workspace externalUserId: "user-456", externalProjectId: "intake-portal-789", }) console.log(sandbox.id) // sbx_f6g7h8i9j0 ``` **Python** ```python sandbox = miosa.sandboxes.create( template_id="miosa-sandbox", wait=True, # hold the call until the sandbox is ready external_workspace_id="acct-123", external_user_id="user-456", external_project_id="intake-portal-789", ) print(sandbox.id) # sbx_f6g7h8i9j0 ``` ### Step 2 - Give your agent an exec tool. The pattern below shows the structure. Substitute `callYourLLM` with your actual model call. **TypeScript** ```typescript // Tool the agent can call async function execInSandbox(command: string): Promise { const result = await sandbox.exec(command) return result.stdout + result.stderr } // Example: agent scaffolds a project const output = await execInSandbox("npx create-react-app /workspace/my-app --template minimal 2>&1 | tail -5") console.log(output) // Success! Created /workspace/my-app // Happy hacking! ``` **Python** ```python def exec_in_sandbox(command: str) -> str: result = sandbox.exec(command) return result.stdout + result.stderr # Example: agent scaffolds a project output = exec_in_sandbox( "npx create-react-app /workspace/my-app --template minimal 2>&1 | tail -5" ) print(output) # Success! Created /workspace/my-app # Happy hacking! ``` ### Step 3 - Let the agent write files directly. **TypeScript** ```typescript // Agent writes a component await sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/my-app/src/App.jsx", `export default function App() { return

Generated by my agent

; }` ) ``` **Python** ```python # Agent writes a component sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/my-app/src/App.jsx", """export default function App() { return

Generated by my agent

; }""", ) ``` ### Step 4 - Start the dev server, create a preview, stream it to your user. **TypeScript** ```typescript // Start the dev server in the background. This call returns right away. await sandbox.exec("nohup npm start > /tmp/app.log 2>&1 &", { cwd: "/workspace/my-app" }) const preview = await sandbox.previews.create(3000) const share = await sandbox.previews.share(preview.id as string) console.log("embed this URL in your product's UI:", share.share_url) // https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai?preview_token=miosa_pv_... ``` **Python** ```python # Start the dev server in the background. This call returns right away. sandbox.processes.start("cd /workspace/my-app && npm start", name="app") preview = sandbox.previews.create(port=3000) share = sandbox.previews.share(preview["id"]) print("embed this URL in your product's UI:", share["share_url"]) # https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai?preview_token=miosa_pv_... ``` The `share_url` is safe to put in an `<iframe>` in your end user's browser. It expires after the configured TTL. Your `msk_*` key never leaves your server. ### Step 5 - Take a screenshot of a Computer (optional). If your agent needs to verify GUI output or run browser-based tasks, use a Computer instead of (or alongside) a Sandbox. **TypeScript** ```typescript const computer = await miosa.computers.create({ name: "agent-desktop", template_type: "miosa-desktop", size: "small", }) // Let the agent observe the screen const png = await computer.desktop.screenshot() // → Buffer containing PNG bytes; send to your vision model // Let the agent interact await computer.desktop.click({ x: 800, y: 400 }) await computer.desktop.type("hello world") await computer.destroy() ``` **Python** ```python computer = miosa.computers.create( name="agent-desktop", template_type="miosa-desktop", size="small", ) # Let the agent observe the screen png = computer.desktop.screenshot() # → bytes containing PNG; send to your vision model # Let the agent interact computer.desktop.click(x=800, y=400) computer.desktop.type("hello world") computer.destroy() ``` ### Step 6 - Publish what the agent built. **TypeScript** ```typescript const result = await sandbox.deploy({ name: "intake-portal", outputPath: "/workspace/my-app/build", }) // Read the production URL from the response; do not construct it. console.log(result) ``` **Python** ```python result = sandbox.deploy( name="intake-portal", output_path="/workspace/my-app/build", ) # Read the production URL from the response; do not construct it. print(result) ``` ### Step 7 - Filter all sandboxes for this customer. **TypeScript** ```typescript const allForCustomer = await miosa.sandboxes.list({ externalWorkspaceId: "acct-123", }) console.log(`${allForCustomer.length} sandboxes for acct-123`) // 3 sandboxes for acct-123 ``` **Python** ```python all_for_customer = miosa.sandboxes.list(external_workspace_id="acct-123") print(f"{len(all_for_customer)} sandboxes for acct-123") # 3 sandboxes for acct-123 ``` ### Step 8 - Clean up. **TypeScript** ```typescript await sandbox.destroy() ``` **Python** ```python sandbox.destroy() ``` ### What you just did | Step | What happened | |------|--------------| | External attribution | Tagged every resource with your customer's IDs - no MIOSA accounts needed for your end users | | Exec as agent tool | Ran arbitrary shell commands inside an isolated VM from your agent loop | | `files.write` | Agent wrote generated code directly to the sandbox file system | | Share token | Minted a browser-safe URL for preview embedding - workspace key stays server-side | | Computer screenshot | Optionally gave the agent a real desktop with a vision-accessible screen | | `sandbox.deploy` | Shipped the agent's output to a permanent immutable URL | | `sandboxes.list` with attribution | Queried only resources belonging to one customer - cross-tenant leakage impossible |
quickstart/app-engine:
Use Docker Host when a workspace needs many always-on apps, funnels, APIs, or client sites without provisioning a separate production VM for each deployment.
The visible product name is Docker Host.
The CLI and API still use `docker_deploy` as the internal compatibility value.

## Step 1  -  Ensure the workspace Docker Host host.

```bash
miosa api POST /docker-deploy/hosts/ensure -d '{"workspace_id": "<workspace-id>"}'
miosa api GET /docker-deploy/hosts
```

The host must be active before an Docker Host publish can finish.

## Step 2  -  Publish the sandbox to Docker Host.

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --name my-app \
  --dir /workspace \
  --run-command "npm run start" \
  --port 3000 \
  --type docker_deploy \
  --wait \
  --wait-timeout 900s \
  --json
```

The response includes the Deployment and its `public_url`.
That URL may be a MIOSA-managed tenant URL, a workspace deployment domain, a tenant deployment domain, or an exact custom domain.
Always show the returned URL.

## Step 3  -  Confirm the app is live.

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment-id> --json
miosa deploy requests <deployment-id>
```

`deploy get` shows the deployment's status, product and `public_url`.
`deploy requests` shows the recent HTTP requests served, so you can confirm real traffic reaches the app.

## What you just did

| Step | What happened |
|------|--------------|
| `docker-deploy ensure` | Created or returned the workspace Docker Host host |
| `sandbox publish --docker-deploy` | Published the sandbox artifact as a container on that workspace host |
| `docker-deploy doctor` | Proved the container and public URL are real |

> **Note: Read more**
>
> See [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy) for the full deployment contract, and [Deploy overview](/docs/docker-host/overview) for the rest of the deploy surface.
quickstart/sandbox-to-deployment:
Start with **Track 1: Sandbox to deployment**. The recommended first walkthrough. Your first success is a small site running at the production URL returned by MIOSA, with its deployment verified. Complete that path before adding agent orchestration or another runtime. > **Building a white-label product?** If your goal is to ship a SaaS where your customers never see the MIOSA brand, start with the [White-Label Integrator Guide](/docs/integrations) instead. It covers per-user provisioning, custom domains, iframe embeds, webhooks, and usage billing from scratch. ## Prerequisites ### Account and workspace Create a MIOSA account at [miosa.ai](https://miosa.ai) and a workspace. ### API key Create a key in Settings → API Keys for the intended workspace. See [API keys](/docs/platform/api-keys) for key types and scopes. Export your key in the terminal where you will run the examples: ```bash export MIOSA_API_KEY="msk_u_..." ``` ### Install tooling for your language **TypeScript** ```bash npm install @miosa/cli @miosa/sdk # or: pnpm add @miosa/cli @miosa/sdk ``` **Python** ```bash pip install --upgrade miosa ``` **Elixir** ```elixir # mix.exs - published on Hex.pm: https://hex.pm/packages/miosa {:miosa, "~> 1.1"} ``` Then run `mix deps.get`. **MCP (Claude Code / Cursor / Windsurf)** **Zero-install option - just a URL + API key:** ```json { "mcpServers": { "miosa": { "url": "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer msk_u_..." } } } } ``` Add this to `~/.claude/mcp.json` (Claude Code), Cursor's MCP settings, or Windsurf's `mcp_config.json`. No pip, no npm - the current capability-scoped tool catalog appears immediately after a client restart. This is the easiest way to get started. **Local server (optional):** ```bash pip install git+https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-mcp.git ``` Or via the TypeScript CLI: ```bash npx @miosa/cli mcp serve ``` > **Caution: Never put msk_* in a browser** > > Workspace API keys are server-only. For browser-side preview embedding, your backend mints a short-lived share token. See [Browser Tokens](/docs/platform/browser-tokens). ## Step 1 - Create a sandbox. **TypeScript** ```typescript import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk" const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! }) const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox", workspaceSlug: "default", // the workspace it belongs to; every create names one }) console.log(sandbox.id, sandbox.state) // sbx_a1b2c3d4e5 running ``` **Python** ```python import os from miosa import Miosa miosa = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"]) sandbox = miosa.sandboxes.create(template_id="miosa-sandbox", workspace_slug="default") print(sandbox.id, sandbox.state) # sbx_a1b2c3d4e5 running ``` ## Step 2 - Write a small static site into `/workspace`. **TypeScript** ```typescript await sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/index.html", ` My App

Hello from MIOSA

Built in a sandbox.

` ) ``` **Python** ```python sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/index.html", """ My App

Hello from MIOSA

Built in a sandbox.

""", ) ``` ## Step 3 - Start a dev server so you can preview it. **TypeScript** ```typescript // Start the dev server. `exec.stream` keeps the process running and yields its output. const events = sandbox.exec.stream("python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0", { cwd: "/workspace" }) for await (const event of events) console.log(event) ``` **Python** ```python # Start the dev server in the background. server = sandbox.commands.run( "python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0", cwd="/workspace", background=True, ) ``` ## Step 4 - Create a preview and open it. **TypeScript** ```typescript const preview = await sandbox.previews.create(3000) console.log(preview.url) // https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` **Python** ```python preview = sandbox.previews.create(port=3000) print(preview.url) # https://5173-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` Open the URL in your browser. You see your `index.html` served live from inside the sandbox. ## Step 5 - Publish to production. **CLI** ```bash miosa deploy create --from-sandbox \ --name my-app \ --dir /workspace \ --type docker_deploy \ --wait \ --json ``` Use the `deployment.id` and `deployment.public_url` returned by MIOSA. **TypeScript** ```typescript const result = await sandbox.deploy({ name: "my-app", outputPath: "/workspace", }) // Read the production URL from the response; do not construct it. console.log(result) ``` **Python** ```python result = sandbox.deploy( name="my-app", output_path="/workspace", ) # Read the production URL from the response; do not construct it. print(result) ``` MIOSA freezes a source snapshot, runs a Builder to package the files, stores an immutable Release, and routes the Deployment URL to it. The sandbox remains alive and editable. ## Step 6 - Prove the deployment. The production URL is the URL returned by MIOSA. Do not construct it from the slug. Use deployment proof when you need an operator or CI check that the app is live. ```bash miosa deploy get --json ``` For Docker Host deployments, proof checks the deployment row, Docker Host host link, host health, durable app target, container route, and public URL probe. ## Step 7 - Make a change and republish. Edit `/workspace/index.html` again and publish to the existing deployment: ```bash miosa deploy create --from-sandbox \ --name \ --dir /workspace \ --type docker_deploy \ --wait \ --json ``` MIOSA creates a new immutable Version and promotes it only after verification succeeds. The previous healthy version remains available for rollback. ## Step 8 - (Optional) Attach a custom domain. See [Domains](/docs/docker-host/domains) for the DNS setup. Short version: add a `CNAME` from your domain to the generated host, hit the verify endpoint, MIOSA issues a TLS certificate. ## Step 9 - Clean up. **TypeScript** ```typescript await sandbox.destroy() ``` **Python** ```python sandbox.destroy() ``` The sandbox is gone. The published deployment and its domain are unaffected - the Release is immutable and lives in object storage independently of the sandbox. ### What you just did | Step | What happened | |------|--------------| | `sandboxes.create` | Created an isolated sandbox on the sandbox image | | `files.write` | Wrote a file into `/workspace` inside the running VM | | `exec` | Ran a command inside the VM over the exec API | | `previews.create` | Opened a tunnel from a public hostname to port 3000 inside the VM | | `sandbox publish` | Froze source, ran Builder, stored Release, created Version, and made it live | | `deploy prove` | Verified that MIOSA can prove the deployment route and runtime state | | `sandbox.destroy` | Terminated the VM; deployment is unaffected | ## What's next - **Add a real backend.** Move from static to dynamic deploys with [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing) and a managed [Postgres database](/docs/data/postgres). - **Authenticate end users.** [Auth-as-a-service](/docs/data/auth) adds a full JWT signup/login flow with one environment variable. - **Roll back a bad deploy.** [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback) repoints the domain at an older version in seconds. - **Understand every primitive.** [Concepts](/docs/concepts) is the canonical architecture reference. - **Build your own product on MIOSA.** The [Platform / White-label overview](/docs/platform/overview) covers preview tokens, share URLs, tenant branding, per-user quotas, webhook subscriptions, Docker Host domains, and the audit log. - **Drop in UI components.** `@miosa/react`, `@miosa/vue`, and `@miosa/svelte` provide `MiosaPreview`, `MiosaTerminal`, `MiosaFileTree`, and `MiosaUsage`. See [UI Components](/docs/ui-components). - **See a full white-label example.** The [reference integration](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa/tree/main/examples) shows a complete platform embedding. - **Extend Claude Code with MIOSA skills.** 5 pre-built skills at [github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-skills](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-skills) give Claude Code sandbox, computer, and deploy primitives. See [Skills](/docs/guides/skills). - **API wire format.** [API Reference](/docs/api-reference) documents every endpoint.
